items.followUp: What is the difference between a saturated and an unsaturated solution?

rubric.why: Assesses the defining feature of a dilute solution.
rubric.description: Identifies a dilute solution as having a relatively small amount of solute.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a dilute solution has little solute compared with the solvent or solution.

rubric.why: Assesses the defining feature of a concentrated solution.
rubric.description: Identifies a concentrated solution as having a relatively large amount of solute.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a concentrated solution has much solute compared with the solvent or solution.

modelAnswer: A dilute solution contains a relatively small amount of solute dissolved in a given amount of solvent.
A concentrated solution contains a relatively large amount of solute dissolved in a given amount of solvent.

items.followUp: Write down any four properties of copper.

rubric.why: Checks knowledge of two characteristic physical properties of silver.
rubric.description: Gives any two valid properties of silver.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any two correct properties; do not award this mark for only one property.

rubric.why: Checks knowledge of two further properties of silver.
rubric.description: Gives two further valid properties of silver.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the remaining two correct properties.

modelAnswer: Silver is lustrous.
Silver is malleable and ductile.
Silver is a good conductor of heat and electricity.

items.followUp: Write the chemical equation for the reaction between hydrogen and oxygen, and name the product.

rubric.why: Assesses the balanced chemical equation for the reaction.
rubric.description: Writes the balanced equation for hydrogen reacting with chlorine.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl.

rubric.why: Assesses the reaction condition and product.
rubric.description: Names hydrogen chloride and states that the reaction occurs in light, often vigorously or explosively.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying hydrogen chloride as the product and mentioning light or sunlight.

modelAnswer: Hydrogen reacts with chlorine in sunlight to form hydrogen chloride.
H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2HCl(g)
The reaction is vigorous and may be explosive in bright sunlight.

items.followUp: Write the equation for the reaction of methane with bromine in diffused sunlight.

rubric.why: Checks the products of methane chlorination.
rubric.description: Shows that methane forms chloromethane and hydrogen chloride.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct products, CH₃Cl and HCl.

rubric.why: Checks the balanced substitution equation and reaction condition.
rubric.description: Writes the balanced equation and identifies diffused sunlight as the condition.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl in diffused sunlight.

modelAnswer: In diffused sunlight, one hydrogen atom of methane is substituted by a chlorine atom.
CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl

items.followUp: State two limitations of Rutherford’s atomic model and one feature of Bohr’s model that addressed them.

rubric.why: Checks Rutherford’s description of the atom’s structure.
rubric.description: States that Rutherford proposed a central nucleus with electrons revolving around it.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the nucleus and revolving electrons.

rubric.why: Checks a key limitation of Rutherford’s model.
rubric.description: States that Rutherford’s model could not explain the stability of the atom.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the stability limitation.

rubric.why: Checks another key limitation of Rutherford’s model.
rubric.description: States that Rutherford’s model could not explain atomic line spectra.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the line-spectrum limitation.

rubric.why: Checks Bohr’s proposed arrangement of electron orbits.
rubric.description: States that Bohr proposed fixed orbits or energy levels for electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for fixed orbits or energy levels.

rubric.why: Checks Bohr’s explanation of atomic stability and spectral lines.
rubric.description: States that electrons do not radiate energy in stationary orbits and that energy is exchanged during transitions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the no-radiation-in-stationary-orbits idea or energy exchange during transitions.

modelAnswer: Rutherford proposed that an atom has a small, positively charged nucleus and electrons revolve around it; most of the atom is empty space.
Rutherford’s theory could not explain why revolving electrons do not lose energy and fall into the nucleus, so it could not explain atomic stability.
Rutherford’s theory could not explain the line spectra of atoms.
Bohr proposed that electrons revolve in fixed orbits, each with a definite energy.
Electrons do not radiate energy while in a stationary orbit; they absorb or emit energy when they move between energy levels.

items.followUp: Define an ionic bond and explain how it forms, giving one example.

rubric.why: Assesses the definition of a covalent bond.
rubric.description: Defines a covalent bond as a bond formed by sharing electron pair(s) between atoms.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for a clear definition involving sharing of one or more pairs of electrons between atoms.

rubric.why: Assesses the single covalent bond and an example.
rubric.description: Explains that a single covalent bond involves one shared pair and gives a valid example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the explanation and an example such as H₂ or Cl₂.

rubric.why: Assesses the double covalent bond and an example.
rubric.description: Explains that a double covalent bond involves two shared pairs and gives an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the explanation and an example such as O₂.

rubric.why: Assesses the triple covalent bond and an example.
rubric.description: Explains that a triple covalent bond involves three shared pairs and gives an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the explanation and an example such as N₂.

modelAnswer: A covalent bond is formed when two atoms share one or more pairs of electrons.
A single covalent bond has one shared pair of electrons; for example, H—H in H₂.
A double covalent bond has two shared pairs of electrons; for example, O=O in O₂.
A triple covalent bond has three shared pairs of electrons; for example, N≡N in N₂.

items.followUp: Define boiling point and state two factors that affect it.

rubric.why: Checks the meaning of vapour pressure.
rubric.description: Defines vapour pressure as the pressure exerted by vapour in equilibrium with its liquid in a closed container.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the equilibrium vapour-pressure definition.

rubric.why: Checks the effect of temperature on vapour pressure.
rubric.description: States that vapour pressure depends on temperature and increases as temperature increases.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming temperature and its increasing effect.

rubric.why: Checks the dependence on the identity of the liquid.
rubric.description: States that vapour pressure depends on the nature of the liquid.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming the nature or kind of liquid.

rubric.why: Checks the role of intermolecular attraction.
rubric.description: Explains that stronger intermolecular forces lower vapour pressure.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking intermolecular forces with vapour pressure.

modelAnswer: Vapour pressure is the pressure exerted by a vapour in equilibrium with its liquid in a closed container.
Vapour pressure depends on temperature; it increases when temperature increases.
It depends on the nature of the liquid.
Stronger intermolecular forces hold molecules in the liquid more strongly and result in a lower vapour pressure.

items.followUp: Write the chemical formula of glucose and water.

rubric.why: Checks recall of the formula of sugar (sucrose).
rubric.description: Gives the chemical formula of sugar, sucrose.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁.

rubric.why: Checks recall of the formula of silicon dioxide.
rubric.description: Gives the chemical formula of silicon dioxide.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for SiO₂.

modelAnswer: Sugar (sucrose): C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁
Silicon dioxide: SiO₂
